- Domain-keyed pools with learned descriptors on a frozen backbone: L2P and CP-Prompt; ProtoDepth (2503.12745) for depth, which is nearly arm M2 already.
- Replay for continual depth: CoDEPS (2303.10147).
- Hypernetworks for continual RNNs: Ehret et al. (2006.12109).
- Prompt tuning of frozen pointmap models: Human3R, Test3R.

Eight searches found no work that tunes, stores or pools CUT3R/TTT3R start states across scenes or domains. None treats a streaming 3D model's initial state as experiential memory. The defensible delta is therefore a question, not a method. A recurrent 3D model overwrites its start state with every frame (fully in CUT3R, gated in TTT3R), and Info3R-style resets restore it partway through a sequence. Two things are unknown:
1. Persistence: does domain experience written into the start state survive the overwrite? We measure it as a gain-vs-frame-index curve and a half-life, under the CUT3R update vs the TTT3R update.
2. What the start state stores: is it more than (a) a cached prefix of in-domain frames (Galim's equivalence predicts it may not be) or (b) a per-domain metric-scale constant?

If it survives and is more than a prefix or scale, the pool result follows: BWT moves from weight drift (one sequential start state) to selection error (the pool). This tests the survey's claim that the short-term/long-term split comes from when formation, evolution and retrieval run: the same tensor is working memory within a scene and, through its initialization, long-term experiential memory across scenes.

What is not novel and should not be claimed:
- pool spawn/merge management;
- learned-key domain selection;
- the hypernetwork generation arm.

The survey-cell framing (Experiential x Latent holds only 2510.09038) is a positioning device, not evidence of novelty.
newIdeas.revised_mechanism:
Backbone: a frozen CUT3R (224 linear for sweeps, 512 DPT for final numbers), run with the CUT3R update rule and with the TTT3R update rule. The only trainable memory is the start state: the initial state tokens (about 1.2 MB in fp16) plus the initial pose token. Gradients flow through the frozen model on 4-8-frame clips.

Two training targets:
- GT, as the oracle;
- self-supervised: first-K-frame predictions from the start state are pulled toward the same model's predictions for those frames after a full TTT3R pass.

The pool holds one start state per domain plus a key.
- Keys: the mean DINOv2 or CUT3R-encoder feature of the first 4 frames, with a ProtoDepth-style learned descriptor as the learned-key variant, and an oracle key as the upper bound.
- Management is kept minimal and is explicitly not the contribution: spawn on a novelty threshold, otherwise update the nearest entry, and merge entries whose outputs differ by less than epsilon.
- Under Info3R-style resets the selected start state is re-applied, so it also acts at every reset, not only at frame 0.

Arms:
- M0: the default start state.
- M1: one start state fine-tuned sequentially across domains.
- M2: the pool, with oracle and learned keys.
- M4: per-domain rank-4 decoder LoRAs at matched bytes.
- M5: one start state trained jointly, or with clip replay.
- G0 (gradient-free): State-Soup-style average of post-warm-up states per domain.

Two new diagnostic baselines decide what the start state actually stores:
- P: a warm-up prefix of N in-domain experience frames fed before the test sequence, with the outputs discarded and the coordinate frame re-anchored. This tests whether the start state is just a compressed prefix.
- S: a per-domain metric-scale scalar applied to the default model's outputs. This tests whether the start state is just scale calibration, especially for KITTI vs indoor.

The hypernetwork arm (M3) is dropped to an optional appendix.

Hypotheses, reduced to three:
- H1: the start state stores more than scale or a prefix. The oracle in-domain start state beats M0, P and S on first-50-frame AbsRel and full-sequence ATE.
- H2: persistence depends on the write rule. The gain half-life is longer under TTT3R than under CUT3R, and is extended by resets.
- H3: forgetting moves to access. M1 has BWT of -3% or worse. M2 has BWT near 0 with oracle keys, and with learned keys at least 80% of its remaining loss falls on misrouted sequences.

H4 (latent vs LoRA by type of shift) is kept as a secondary map. Galim et al. predict that LoRA wins overall.
newIdeas.revised_first_experiment:
About 15 GPU-hours over 2 weeks, on CUT3R-224 with two domains, KITTI and Bonn (add ScanNet if time allows).
- For each domain, tune the start state with GT targets and with self-supervised targets on 10 experience sequences (1,000 steps, 8-frame clips, 2 seeds, about 0.3 GPU-hours per run).
- On held-out in-domain and cross-domain sequences, compare against:
  - M0, the default start state;
  - P, the warm-up prefix (N = 8, 32);
  - S, the per-domain scale scalar;
  - G0, the averaged post-warm-up state.
- Run each comparison under both the CUT3R update rule and the TTT3R update rule.
- Report per-frame AbsRel gain curves, the half-life of the gain, first-50-frame and full-sequence AbsRel/ATE, and one check at 512 resolution for the best setting.

GO if all four hold:
1. In at least one domain, the oracle start state improves first-50-frame AbsRel by at least 8% and full-sequence AbsRel or ATE by at least 3% over M0.
2. It beats the better of P and S by at least 3% on first-50-frame AbsRel.
3. The cross-domain start state is worse than M0.
4. Self-supervised tuning recovers at least 50% of the oracle gain.
newIdeas.revised_kill_criterion:
Kill the whole card in any of these cases:
- The oracle start state improves first-50-frame AbsRel by less than 3% in both domains.
- The gain half-life is under about 10 frames under TTT3R even with resets. The overwrite then erases the experience. Report this as a negative boundary note and give the experience question to #7's adapters.
- P or S comes within 1% of the tuned start state. The start state would then be a cached prefix or a scale constant, not experiential memory.

Kill only the pool part, keeping a single-prior note, if one jointly trained start state (M5) comes within 1% of the per-domain states.

Pause if self-supervised tuning recovers less than 25% of the oracle gain.

original.title: Experience in the initial state: a continual pool of learned start states for streaming 3D across deployments
original.one_liner: Every scene CUT3R/TTT3R reconstructs starts from the same learned initial state tokens, so an agent deployed for months never reuses what earlier scenes taught it. Keep that experience as a pool of domain-tuned start states with the backbone frozen. Either retrieve one at the first frame (L2P-style) or generate one with a tiny hypernetwork (MemGen-style). Compare against a per-domain LoRA at matched bytes.
original.survey_cell: Experiential x Latent, the sparsest cell in the survey list: one paper, 'Auto-scaling Continuous Memory for GUI Agent'. The study compares forms (a latent start-state pool vs a parametric LoRA vs a data buffer of replayed clips) and retrieval vs generation (survey 7.1).
original.survey_hook: The survey defines experiential memory as knowledge carried across tasks, from case-based to strategy-based, and notes a growing emphasis on memory that transfers across tasks. Yet its experiential-latent cell holds a single paper, and every embodied or spatial memory in its list (Mem2Ego, Embodied VideoAgent, MemoryVLA, Context as Memory) is factual memory about the current scene. The survey's 'latent repository' (MemoryLLM, M+, MemoryVLA) and 'latent memory generation' (the MemGen weaver) supply the two arms. The survey also says short-term and long-term memory arise from when F/E/R run, not from separate modules. Here the same state tensor is working memory within a scene, while its initialization is long-term experiential memory across scenes.
original.big_picture_hook:
- It moves the doc's weights row (L2P prompt pools) into a 3D recurrent model.
- 'Forgetting tracks how far an update moves the model': tuning only the start state moves no weights, so forgetting can only return through picking the wrong pool entry. That directly tests the doc's lesson that external memory moves the dilemma to memory access.
- Harrington et al. (2607.07847) found that the kind of change decides whether adaptation needs the weights. Here the test is which domain shifts (camera and scale statistics, scene dynamics, indoor vs driving layout) a start state can absorb and which need a LoRA.
- It extends the doc's 3D section beyond single scenes. TTT3R's fast state is lost per session; #2 and #7 keep individual scenes, while this card keeps the experience of having reconstructed many.
original.task:
Domain-incremental streaming reconstruction where the domain is not labeled.
- Stream of domains for a frozen CUT3R/TTT3R: ScanNet (indoor handheld) -> KITTI (driving) -> Bonn RGB-D (dynamic indoor) -> TUM/7-Scenes (office, different camera) -> ScanNet again (A-B-A). Each domain has 10-20 experience sequences and held-out test sequences.
- Checkpoints: cut3r_224_linear_4.pth for sweeps and cut3r_512_dpt_4_64.pth for final numbers, both with the TTT3R update rule.
- Metrics:
  - video depth AbsRel and delta<1.25 (Bonn, KITTI, ScanNet) and ATE/RPE (TUM, ScanNet, KITTI), each over the first 50 frames (where the start state matters most) and over the full sequence;
  - a domain accuracy matrix with average accuracy, backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT);
  - the pool's retrieval accuracy against the true domain.
original.mechanism:
- Formation: tune only the start state, i.e. CUT3R's learnable initial state tokens (768x768, about 1.2 MB in fp16) plus the initial pose token. Gradients flow through the frozen model on 4-8-frame clips.
  - Self-supervised target, no labels needed: the predictions from the start state on the first K frames should match the same model's predictions for those frames after it has seen the full sequence (a second TTT3R pass).
  - GT target: gives the oracle upper bound.
- Pool management: the key is the mean DINOv2 (or CUT3R encoder) feature of the first frames. Spawn a new entry when novelty passes a threshold; otherwise update the nearest entry. Merge entries whose start states produce near-identical outputs (consolidation).
- Arms:
  - M0: the default start state.
  - M1: one start state fine-tuned sequentially across domains (expected to forget).
  - M2: the pool with key retrieval, with both oracle-key and learned-key variants.
  - M3 (generation): a hypernetwork that maps first-frame features to a low-rank change in the start state, trained continually with a small replay of keys.
  - M4: a per-domain pool of rank-4 decoder LoRAs at matched bytes, plus one shared VPT prompt (Human3R-style).
  - M5: one start state trained with a clip replay buffer.
  - A gradient-free baseline: a State-Soup-style average of post-warm-up states.
original.hypothesis:
- H1 (experience fits in the start state): in at least 3 of 5 domains, an in-domain tuned start state improves held-out first-50-frame AbsRel by at least 8% and full-sequence ATE by at least 3%. A start state tuned on a mismatched domain is worse than the default, so a pool, and its management, is necessary.
- H2 (forgetting moves to access): the single sequential start state (M1) shows BWT of -3% or worse. The pool (M2) shows BWT near 0 with oracle keys; with learned keys, at least 80% of its remaining loss falls on misrouted sequences.
- H3 (generation vs retrieval): the hypernetwork (M3) beats retrieval on held-out mixed conditions (for example TUM dynamic sequences), but forgets more under sequential training.
- H4 (latent vs weights): the start-state pool comes within 2% of the LoRA pool on camera and scale shifts, but loses by at least 5% on dynamics (Bonn). This maps where experience needs weights.
original.first_experiment:
About 12 GPU-hours over 2 weeks.
- Setup: CUT3R-224 with TTT3R on two domains, KITTI and Bonn/TUM.
- Tune the start state per domain with GT (oracle) targets and with self-supervised targets: 10 experience sequences, 1,000 steps on 8-frame clips, 2 seeds, about 0.3 GPU-hours per run.
- Evaluate on held-out sequences, both in-domain and cross-domain, then check the best setting once at 512 resolution.
- GO if all three hold:
  - in at least one domain, the oracle in-domain start state improves first-50-frame AbsRel by at least 8% and full-sequence AbsRel or ATE by at least 3%;
  - the cross-domain start state is worse than the default;
  - self-supervised tuning recovers at least 50% of the oracle gain.
original.kill_criterion:
- Kill if the oracle-tuned start state improves first-50-frame AbsRel by less than 3% in both domains. TTT3R would then overwrite the start state too quickly for experience to live there. That is a reportable boundary, and the experience question passes to #7-style adapters.
- Kill the pool-management part, keeping only a single-prior result, if one start state tuned jointly on all domains comes within 1% of per-domain start states.
- Pause if self-supervised tuning recovers less than 25% of the oracle gain, because the method would then need labels a deployed agent does not have.

newIdeas.differentiation:
What is taken:
(a) Deletion. Store-only deletion leaving the weight copy leakable is close to tautological. Agentic Unlearning (2602.17692, 'backflow' plus synchronized unlearning), LMLM/Co-LMLM and CURE already cover it. H3's first clause adds nothing.

(c) Global effect of fine-tuning. Context-Parametric Inversion (2410.10796) shows fine-tuning reduces context reliance in general.
(d) The failure itself. 2404.01652 already describes 'hard-coded' readers that resist corpus updates.
(e) Internal overlap. 'P(change) x coherence cost, paid at write time' is the expiry term of shortlist #9, and the store-deletion step is #3.

What survives, since 8 searches found no paper sweeping consolidation strength against override of a fresher store copy:
(1) A controlled dose-response, SOR(s), for facts with no pretraining prior (fictitious TOFU authors), consolidated by LoRA vs full SFT, with the new value in retrieved context.
(2) A decomposition of SOR into three parts: the fact's own no-context margin (the ClashEval law); a per-fact 'consolidation' residual at matched margin (consolidated facts vs pretrained facts vs store-only control authors in the same run); and a global loss of context reliance caused by the SFT (the 2410.10796 effect, measured on never-consolidated control facts).
(3) Revival: after write-through to the new value, does retrieving the old raw log bring the old value back?

newIdeas.revised_mechanism:
The question: when a fact has two copies (store text and consolidated weights) and the store copy changes, what decides whether the store still wins, and what is the cheapest repair?

Decomposition model. Fit a per-query logistic model:
logit P(stale) = a*margin_old + b*consolidated + c*s + d*global_inversion(run) + e*(note present)
- margin_old: the no-context log-prob margin of the old value.
- consolidated: whether the fact went through the consolidation SFT.
- s: consolidation strength in epochs.
- global_inversion(run): the SOR on never-consolidated control facts in that run.
The ClashEval prior predicts that a alone explains most of the variance. The card's claim is that b>0 at matched margin: consolidation leaves debt that the read-time margin does not show (for example a rote, context-insensitive retrieval path). The alternative is that d dominates, meaning the SFT run as a whole becomes less context-reliant. Each outcome points to a different fix:
- b dominates: price debt per fact (#9).
- d dominates: price debt per write batch, and add context-conflict replay during consolidation.
- a dominates: debt equals margin, so the margin can be read off directly at write time.

Protocols:
- P0: store only.
- P1: supersession note ('updated: X is now B, not A').
- P2: write-through by LoRA SFT on the new value. An AlphaEdit write is optional and reuses #1's setup.
- P4: margin-gated. Use P1 if the predicted SOR from the fitted model is below theta, otherwise P2. Calibrate theta on 20% of facts.
- Deletion: only P3, a gradient-difference unlearning step, is run. The measurement is the unlearning KL needed to reach the retain-model leakage floor (CURE-style retain baseline, not the never-trained base), regressed on consolidation KL at write time.

Dropped:
- The latent soft-prompt arm and the KV-prefix control: a third copy that dilutes the claim.
- Lazy write-back (P5): it is #9's policy, not a measurement.

Output to #9: an expiry cost per fact, E[cost | change] = P(stale | protocol) x error cost + protocol writes x KL per write. The cost is predictable at write time from the margin, update norm and consolidation KL.

original.title: Consolidation debt: does the store still win after a consolidated fact changes or is deleted?
original.one_liner: Consolidate TOFU facts into a model of 1.5B or smaller at a controlled strength. Then change or delete those facts in the text store only, and measure how often the stale copy in the weights overrides the fresh store copy, or leaks after deletion. Test whether a margin measured at write time predicts this, and whether it can choose the cheapest repair: a note in context, writing the new value through to the weights, or invalidating the old one.
original.survey_cell: Factual x Parametric and Factual x Token-level together (one fact held in two forms), under the Evolution operator E (Updating and Forgetting), plus the trustworthy-memory frontier (deletion). A small latent arm uses a soft-prompt memory.
original.survey_hook: The survey treats updating as conflict resolution for external stores and as model editing for parametric memory, but never asks whether the two copies stay consistent. The third-party critique in the digest names this blind spot: the weights and the database fall out of sync as both change. The trustworthy-memory frontier asks for privacy and robustness to leakage, which in practice means deletion. Closest prior work, from search snippets only: Agentic Unlearning (2602.17692) already unlearns across parameters and memory together. It calls the failure 'parameter-memory backflow' and reports forget-set MedQA accuracy falling from 78% to 14% (its own numbers). The Always-On Agents survey (2606.30306) says a forget request must reach every derived tier. Adjacent conflict studies: 2609.24238 and 2410.05162. None of the results directly tests stale fine-tuned weights overriding a fresher store copy as a function of how strongly the fact was consolidated, and none covers value updates as opposed to deletion.
original.big_picture_hook: The doc's open problem is consolidation: what should move from context or the store into the weights, and when. This card asks the other half: what does it cost when a fact that moved later changes or must be deleted? The doc's lesson that 'forgetting tracks how far an update moves the model' (sparse memory finetuning, RL's Razor) predicts that this cost grows with the KL shift the consolidation write caused. Memini's coupled fast and slow variables give the same entrenchment in an external store. The result turns the doc's consolidation question into a priced decision: P(change) x coherence cost, paid at write time.
original.task:
Data and models:
- TOFU (locuslab/TOFU): 200 fictitious authors x 20 QA each.
- Consolidated into Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct by LoRA (r=16) and by full SFT, at strength s in {1, 3, 5, 10} epochs.
- Half the authors are left store-only as a control.
- Text store: the same QA and bio text in a bge-small index, top-3 retrieval.

Change stream:
- 400 facts get a new value: the store is updated, the weights are not.
- 200 facts get a deletion request: the store text is removed.

Second route: AlphaEdit/MEMIT edits of CounterFact facts on GPT2-XL or phi-1.5 (the setup from card #1).

Metrics:
- Current-value accuracy (CVA): the new value is output when its text is retrieved.
- Stale-override rate (SOR): the old value is output even though the new text is in context.
- Revival rate: after the weights are edited to the new value, an old raw log is retrieved and the old value comes back.
- Deletion leakage: the old value appears under no-context, paraphrase and retrieval-style prompts, relative to the rate for a never-trained base model.
- Locality: accuracy on retained authors, and KL on WikiText-103 validation.
- Weight writes per change.
original.mechanism:
Coherence protocols for a fact whose copies live in two or three forms, borrowing the cache-coherence analogy:
- P0: update the store only.
- P1: add a supersession note in context ('updated: X is now B, not A').
- P2 (write-through): a LoRA SFT or AlphaEdit write of the new value.
- P3 (invalidate): gradient-difference unlearning of the old value, or an edit toward an 'unknown' target.
- P4 (margin-gated): before the change, measure the no-context log-prob margin of the old value over alternatives. Use P1 if the margin is below theta, otherwise P2 or P3. Calibrate theta on 20% of facts.
- P5 (lazy): batched write-back at the next consolidation round.

Latent arm: an 8-32-vector soft prompt fit to each batch of 20 authors, as in card #3's soft-prompt address. Measure leakage when the prefix is not refit after a deletion, and the cost of refitting it from the store, so that the store acts as the source of truth. A cached KV prefix of the memory block serves as an exact-by-recompute control. The expected failures are in forms that merge many items (the weights, a jointly fit prompt), not in caches that are a pure function of text.

Predictors logged at write time: epochs, LoRA update norm, consolidation KL on generic text, and the no-context margin. Compare them with the LoRA memorization law in 2605.30260 if its form applies.
original.hypothesis:
H1: SOR rises with consolidation strength. At s=10 on the 1.5B model, SOR is at least 25% under P0 and at least 10% under P1.

H2: The margin measured before the change predicts each fact's SOR with AUROC of at least 0.75. P4 reaches at least 95% of write-through CVA with at most 40% of its weight writes and at most half its locality loss.

H3: Deleting from the store alone leaves leakage close to the undeleted level. The KL needed to bring leakage down to the never-trained base rate correlates with the consolidation KL at write time (Spearman of at least 0.5). This makes consolidation debt predictable when the fact is first written.
original.first_experiment:
About 8 GPU-h over 1-2 weeks:
- LoRA-consolidate 100 TOFU authors into Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B at s in {1, 3, 10}: 6 runs, about 0.3 GPU-h each.
- Apply 400 updates and 200 deletions under P0 and P1 only.
- Measure SOR, revival and leakage against s, and the AUROC of the margin.

GO if all three hold for at least one model:
- SOR under P0 is at least 15% at the highest strength;
- SOR rises with s (Spearman over facts of at least 0.3);
- the margin's AUROC is at least 0.7.
original.kill_criterion:
Kill if, for both models at every strength, SOR stays under 5% with the new text in context and leakage after store-only deletion stays within 3 points of the never-trained base. That would mean small models simply follow the context, so coherence costs nothing at this scale.

Kill, or shrink to the update-only half, if a full read of Agentic Unlearning (2602.17692) or 2609.24238 shows they already report override rate against consolidation strength.

newIdeas.title: Learned writing or learned deciding? A swap-based audit of released RL memory managers under change-rate shift
newIdeas.one_liner: This is an inference-only audit of the released Mem-alpha-4B and RL-MemAgent-7B checkpoints. A 2x2 prefix-forced swap (RL vs rule operation choice, RL vs base written content) measures how much of the RL gain comes from WHAT is written rather than WHICH operation is chosen. The policies are then stressed on a CPU-generated stream whose per-fact change hazard moves away from training, against a self-recalibrating rule and training-free managers.

closest_work.title: Memory-R1: Enhancing LLM Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via RL (ACL 2026)
closest_work.overlap: This is the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP manager trained with RL. Its component ablation removes the manager or the answer agent but never swaps in a heuristic manager while keeping the RL parts. An informal referee note (https://pith.science/paper/2508.19828) flags exactly this missing heuristic or non-RL manager ablation. That confirms the gap, but it also shows the gap is visible to others.

closest_work.title: Mem-alpha: Learning Memory Construction via Reinforcement Learning
closest_work.overlap: This is the primary audit target. Its ablations vary only the reward weights (gamma=0 collapses performance) and compare against the base Qwen3-4B and gpt-4.1-mini with the same tools. There is no rule baseline and no split between operation and content. It claims to generalize from 30k-token training to over 400k tokens, so length shift alone is partly covered.

closest_work.title: MINTEval: Evaluating Memory under Multi-Target Interference
closest_work.overlap: This already logs Mem-alpha's (and AtomMem's) operation types. Inserts are 65.9% of Mem-alpha's operations, and the agents fail to recognise revisions as updates. closest_work.title: What Should an Agent Forget? Separating What Is Stored from What Is Used (RD-Forget)
closest_work.overlap: This is a training-free manager: a frozen-LLM curator, semantic slots and replacement links, evaluated on fact consolidation and knowledge updating. It partly shows that no RL is needed for the management layer. It must be included as a baseline arm. If it already beats Mem-alpha on FactConsolidation, H1's headline is weakened.

closest_work.overlap: Its no-RL ablation uses a prompted writer, which beats the backbone but degrades with length. It reports robustness across memory sizes. It has no operation layer, so for this agent the audit can only test content. There is no extractive or cross-encoder overwrite baseline.

closest_work.overlap: This diagnoses the update or supersession gap. GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B raises supersession accuracy from 9.0% to 16.7% in a single run. It attributes the gain to the policy, but has no rule baseline and no change-rate shift.

closest_work.title: Memory as a Controlled Process (MemCon)
closest_work.overlap: A lightweight learned (bandit-style) controller is competitive. That is evidence that heavy RL is not needed for the decision layer, but MemCon does not audit released RL checkpoints.

newIdeas.differentiation:
What is taken:
- Operation-frequency logging of Mem-alpha, which is mostly inserts and misses updates (MINTEval 2605.18565).
- Hand overwrite rules on selective forgetting for a prompted agent (MemoryAgentBench appendix).
- Training-free managers that compete on fact consolidation (RD-Forget 2609.10263, Janus 2606.31121).
- Lightweight learned controllers (MemCon).
- The general point that memory-system gains are often driven by implementation details (2601.01280).
- The specific complaint that Memory-R1 lacks a heuristic-manager ablation, which a public referee note already raises, so the gap is visible to others.
- Length extrapolation, which Mem-alpha and MemAgent already report.

What none of the snippets show, and what is still defensible:
1. A causal swap on the released RL checkpoints that separates operation choice from written content. This is a 2x2 with prefix-forced decoding, measured as the fraction of RL gain retained with prevalence-adjusted agreement. It answers 'what did RL learn' rather than 'is RL better'.
2. A controlled shift in the per-fact change hazard h, independent of length, with the frozen RL policy against a rule that re-estimates its threshold online. This stability-plasticity probe ties directly to the big-picture doc's third lesson and is absent from all the hits.
3. A head-to-head of RL managers against current training-free managers (RD-Forget, Janus-wrapped base, a cross-encoder extractive overwrite) at matched memory tokens and LLM calls.

Weaknesses:
- MemAgent has no operation layer, so for it the audit is content-only.
- The MINTEval prior means a high raw kappa is unsurprising. Agreement must be reported on non-INSERT decisions.
- The swap may create off-distribution prefixes. Parse-failure and refusal rates must be reported.
newIdeas.revised_mechanism:
Everything is inference-only on frozen checkpoints, with vLLM and one 48-80 GB GPU.

(0) Provenance gate. Confirm that the YuWangX/Memalpha-4B card cites 2509.25911 and names its base (reportedly Qwen3-4B). Also confirm that BytedTsinghua-SIA/RL-MemoryAgent-7B is paired with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Check the MemFactory release for a usable Memory-R1 manager checkpoint. If one exists, add it as a third arm. If not, Memory-R1 enters only through its published ablation.

(a) Log Mem-alpha. Record every tool call: operation, target (core, semantic or episodic) and content. Use MemoryAgentBench accurate retrieval, FactConsolidation-SH/MH, and a CPU-generated entity-attribute stream in FactConsolidation format.

(b) The 2x2 swap. Cross {operation: RL | rule} with {content: RL | base}.
- Implementation: prefix-force the tool name and target, then let the other model decode the arguments, or the reverse.
- Two rules:
  - R-tree: a tree of depth 3 or less, fit to Mem-alpha's logged operations. Features: the maximum bge-small similarity to existing entries, NLI contradiction with the nearest entry, and chunk novelty.
  - R-hand: UPDATE above a similarity threshold, replace on NLI contradiction, otherwise INSERT, with LRU eviction at the budget. The replacement step is optionally the BOCPD gate from card #10.
- Report:
  - fraction of RL gain retained = (Acc_variant - Acc_base) / (Acc_RL - Acc_base), with paired-bootstrap CIs;
  - Cohen's kappa overall AND restricted to non-INSERT decisions (the MINTEval prior);
  - parse-failure rate of swapped calls.

(c) Training-free comparators at matched memory tokens and LLM calls:
- RD-Forget, if code is released;
- base Qwen3-4B wrapped by a Janus-style accept/reject gate;
- MemoryAgentBench's always-prefer-later overwrite;
- BM25/bge top-k over raw chunks (brute force).

(d) MemAgent, content only. A cross-encoder extractive overwrite keeps the sentences most relevant to (question + current memory) within the same fixed memory length (verify 1,024 tokens). The gold-supporting-sentence oracle bounds the headroom. Use RULER-HotpotQA at 28k, 112k and 448k.

(e) Shift sweep, the main new axis.
- Hazard h is in {0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3} per fact per chunk, at fixed length 100k. Length is swept separately (30k to 400k) at a fixed h.
- R-hand re-estimates its contradiction threshold online from the observed contradiction rate. The RL policies stay frozen.
- Read out:
  - the slope of current-value accuracy against h;
  - the stale-answer rate;
  - DELETE+INSERT fragmentation.
newIdeas.revised_first_experiment:
About 16 GPU-h over 2 weeks.

Week 1, about 10 GPU-h:
- Run the provenance gate.
- Run Mem-alpha-4B and Qwen3-4B on 100 MemoryAgentBench instances (accurate retrieval plus FactConsolidation-SH) and on 50 synthetic streams at h in {0, 0.3}.
- Log the operations, fit R-tree, and run the full 2x2 swap with R-tree and R-hand.
- Add the always-prefer-later rule and BM25 top-k at matched tokens.

Week 2, about 6 GPU-h:
- Run RL-MemoryAgent-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 128 RULER-HotpotQA questions at 28k and 112k.
- Add the extractive overwrite and the gold oracle.

GO if paired-bootstrap CIs exclude zero and at least one of these holds:
- (i) rule-operation + RL-content keeps at least 70% of Mem-alpha's gain, while RL-operation + base-content keeps 40% or less. This is the 'learned writing' story.
- (ii) at h=0.3, Mem-alpha's current-value accuracy drop relative to h=0 exceeds R-hand's drop by at least 5 points. This is the 'frozen policy is brittle to change rate' story.
- (iii) the extractive overwrite keeps at least 60% of MemAgent's gain at 112k.

Before reading the results, also check whether RD-Forget's reported FactConsolidation numbers already exceed Mem-alpha's. If they do, reframe the paper around (ii) and (b), not around 'rules suffice'.
newIdeas.revised_kill_criterion:
Kill if all four hold:
- In the 2x2, both rule-operation arms keep under 40% of Mem-alpha's gain, AND base-content with RL-operations also keeps under 40% (gain is not separable; it lives in the interaction).
- The extractive overwrite keeps under 30% of MemAgent's gain.
- The RL policy's degradation from h=0 to h=0.3 is within 2 points of the online rule's.
- Non-INSERT kappa between R-tree and Mem-alpha is below 0.3.

That would mean RL learned a joint decision-and-writing policy that cheap rules cannot reproduce and that is not brittle to change rate. That outcome supports Section 7.3. It is reportable as a short negative note, not a paper.

Also stop at the gate if:
- the Memalpha-4B card does not tie the checkpoint to 2509.25911;
- swapped prefix-forced calls fail to parse more than 15% of the time;
- a paper appears that runs a heuristic-manager swap on Mem-alpha or Memory-R1 (watch the pith critique thread and the MINTEval authors).

original.title: What did RL learn to remember? Separating operation choice from written content in RL-trained memory managers, and testing them under stream shift
original.one_liner: Split the gain of released RL memory managers (Mem-alpha-4B, RL-MemAgent-7B) into two parts: which memory operation is chosen, and what text gets written. Replace the operation policy with a rule that uses three features or fewer, and a training-free overwrite. Then shift the stream's change rate and length away from training and see whether the frozen RL policy or the rule degrades more.
original.survey_cell: Factual and Working x Token-level, RL-enabled memory. Frontier sections 7.2 (automated memory management) and 7.3 (RL meets agent memory).
original.survey_hook: Sections 7.2 and 7.3 call for moving from handcrafted heuristics to learned, policy-driven management. They name Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MEM1 and MemAgent as the RL route. The third-party critique says the survey has a complexity bias and undervalues brute-force baselines. A search (snippets only) found no matched-condition comparison of an RL manager against a well-tuned rule-based manager. Memory-R1's own ablation, as summarized in search results, moves the manager's F1 only to 24.6-24.9, while the answer agent goes from 20.5 to 37.5. That suggests much of the gain lies outside the operation policy. MemAgent's no-RL ablation used a prompted LLM writer, not a principled rule. Fine-Mem (2601.08435) argues that outcome-only rewards give poor credit assignment, and MemCon (2607.13591) wins with a lightweight bandit.
original.big_picture_hook: The doc's third lesson is that external memory moves the stability-plasticity dilemma to memory access. For a store, the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP choice is exactly that dial. Harrington et al. (2607.07847) found that online RL handled knowledge updates best but was fragile under noisy rewards. A frozen RL-trained manager is itself a learned component, and it goes out of distribution when the stream's change rate or length shifts. The doc's first lesson, that storage was never the real constraint and brute-force replay is strong, motivates a brute-force arm at matched tokens.
original.task:
Benchmarks:
1. MemoryAgentBench (2507.05257) with Mem-alpha: accurate retrieval, long-range understanding, and selective forgetting via FactConsolidation-SH/MH.
2. RULER-HotpotQA at 28k, 112k and 448k tokens with MemAgent, the setting in its paper.
3. A CPU-generated entity-attribute stream in FactConsolidation format. Change hazard h is in {0, 0.1, 0.3} per fact per chunk, and length runs from 30k to 400k, so change rate and length shift independently.

Metrics:
- Official accuracy/EM per competency.
- Fraction of the RL gain retained: (Acc_variant - Acc_base) / (Acc_RL - Acc_base).
- Cohen's kappa between the rule's and the RL policy's operation choices.
- Memory tokens and LLM calls.
- Operation-level errors, such as DELETE+ADD fragmentation.
original.mechanism:
Checkpoints:
- YuWangX/Memalpha-4B, listed on a model mirror under Mem-alpha's first author. Confirm the card links it to 2509.25911 and names its base model, reportedly Qwen3-4B. Compare against that base.
- BytedTsinghua-SIA/RL-MemoryAgent-7B (Apache-2.0, 32k context), compared against Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
- No official Memory-R1 checkpoint was found, so it enters only through its published ablation.

Steps:
(a) Log every memory tool call Mem-alpha makes: operation, target (core, semantic or episodic) and content.
(b) Run a 2x2 swap with prefix-forced decoding in vLLM: {operation policy: RL or rule} x {content writer: RL or base}. Two rules are tested:
   - a tree of depth 3 or less, fit to Mem-alpha's own logged operations on three cheap features: the maximum bge-small similarity to existing entries, NLI contradiction with the nearest entry, and chunk novelty;
   - a hand rule: UPDATE when similarity passes a threshold, replace on NLI contradiction, otherwise ADD, with LRU eviction at the budget.
(c) For MemAgent, a training-free overwrite: keep the sentences most relevant to (question + current memory) under a cross-encoder, within the same fixed memory length (1,024 tokens in the paper's setup; verify). An oracle that keeps the gold supporting sentences bounds the headroom.
(d) Brute-force arm: BM25/bge top-k over the raw chunks at matched context tokens.
(e) Shift sweeps over hazard and length. The hand rule re-estimates its threshold online from the observed contradiction rate; the RL policy stays frozen.

Optional arm: a tabular bandit in the style of MemCon as a cheap learned controller.
original.hypothesis:
H1: At least 60% of Mem-alpha's gain over its base comes from the content writer, not the operation policy. The tree matches the RL operation choices at kappa of at least 0.6, and rule operations with RL content keep at least 70% of the gain.

H2: When the change rate shifts to h=0.3 and length grows 10x, the RL operation policy loses at least 5 points more than the online rule on selective forgetting.

H3: The training-free overwrite keeps at least 60% of RL-MemAgent's gain over its base at 112k tokens.

If all three hold, the 'learned management' in these systems is mostly learned writing, and the decision layer can be a principled, self-recalibrating rule.

newIdeas.title: Is a memory tier just a recency prior? Replaying identical memory content to compare tiered memory with timing-only routing at swept query delays
newIdeas.one_liner: Run each tiered agent memory once and log every formed item along with when it entered and left each tier: a FIFO buffer plus a store, a MemGPT-style curated core block plus an archive, and LightMem. Then replay that identical content at queries placed at controlled delays after the evidence. This tests whether a timing-only rule (a recency quota, or ACT-R-style activation) reproduces both the tier's membership and its accuracy. The survey claims short- and long-term memory differ only in when formation, evolution and retrieval run. This is a test of that claim at the routing layer, with content held fixed.

newIdeas.differentiation:
Eight searches found no published ablation that holds memory content fixed and compares tiers against a single store with timing-only routing. Three things are already published:
- the controlled-decomposition method (2601.01280, MemDelta 2606.29914, 2606.24775);
- recency decay on LongMemEval and its trade-off between knowledge-update and cross-session questions (LiCoMemory 2511.01448);
- tier-level ablations that remove a tier together with its content (ENGRAM 2511.12960, HiMem 2601.06377, AgeMem, 2603.29194).

The original design has two weaknesses, and either could sink it.

(a) For T-A, H1 holds by construction. A FIFO buffer of K turns over cached items is exactly a recency quota with q = K, so T-A can only serve as a check that the harness reproduces itself.

(b) LongMemEval and LoCoMo ask every question at the end of the stream. The working tier at question time is then just the tail of the last session, so the tier boundary barely enters, and the null outcome that the kill criterion fears becomes likely. MEMTIER already reports that LoCoMo is insensitive, and 2601.01280 finds that foundational settings dominate.

What remains defensible:
1. Content-matched replay: one formation pass is logged with each item's tier-entry and tier-exit times, so routing is separated from formation.
2. A sweep over query delay. Each question is asked at several delays after its evidence session, by snapshotting the replayed store, so the claim that a tier is a timescale is tested on time itself.
3. A cheap membership test that runs on CPU: can timing features (formation age, re-access count, ACT-R activation) decode which items an agent-curated core block holds, scored as AUC, and is any undecodable remainder the part that carries accuracy?
4. A schedule-versus-routing variance decomposition, which directly tests the survey's F/E/R claim.

The survey quote itself was never checked against the PDF, only through search snippets. Verify it before framing the paper around it.
newIdeas.revised_mechanism:
Harness:
- Formation and consolidation run once per system and schedule. Use gpt-4o-mini by API, to stay within the at-most-1.5B / API-only constraint, with Qwen2.5-1.5B as a local cross-check. The embedder is bge-small, and one fixed API reader answers all questions.
- Every formed item is logged with its formation time, every write-time similarity hit (counted as a re-access), and its tier-membership intervals.

Systems:
- T-A: FIFO buffer plus a store. A sanity check only: route (iii) with q = K must reproduce it exactly.
- T-B: a MemGPT/Letta-style core block of at most B tokens, edited by the agent, plus an archive. This is the main object of study.
- T-C: LightMem's released short-term/long-term pipeline, if it runs; otherwise drop it.

Schedules: consolidation every tau_E sessions, with tau_E in {1, 4, end-only}.

Routes, applied to the identical cached items at query time t:
- (i) the original tiers;
- (ii) a single store with similarity top-k;
- (iii) (ii) plus a quota of the q most recently formed items;
- (iv) (ii) plus ACT-R base-level activation, B = ln of the sum over j of (t - t_j)^-d;
- (v) (ii) plus an oracle quota that reserves exactly the items the tier held at time t, but ranks them by similarity, separating membership from placement.

The temporal rules have at most 2 parameters, fit on a dev split. All routes share one context-token budget.

Delay-swept probe: rebuild LongMemEval-S streams so that each question is also asked at delays of {0, 1, 4, 16, end} sessions after its last evidence session. This is cheap, because snapshots replay the cached log with no new formation calls.

Analyses:
1. Accuracy-equivalence curves as a function of delay.
2. The AUC with which timing features predict T-B core-block membership.
3. Eta squared of schedule against route.
4. Per-category stability and plasticity: early-evidence accuracy against knowledge-update and temporal-reasoning accuracy.

LoCoMo is dropped as a primary benchmark because it is insensitive to architecture. Use it only as a sanity check.
newIdeas.revised_first_experiment:
About 6 GPU-hours for embeddings and local cross-checks, plus about $40 of API:
1. Run T-B (core block plus archive) at end-only and tau_E = 1 on 150 LongMemEval-S questions, logging formation and membership.
2. Build the delay-swept probe at delays {0, 4, end}.
3. Evaluate routes (ii) to (v), and route (i) for T-B.
4. Compute the core-membership AUC from timing features.

GO if all of the following hold:
- Some pair of routes differs by at least 3 points at some delay, which shows the probe is sensitive to routing.
- The paired-bootstrap half-width is at most 2 points.
- One of these two outcomes holds:
  - Support: the best temporal rule comes within 2 points of the tier at every delay, and the timing AUC is at least 0.8.
  - Refutation: the tier beats every temporal rule by at least 4 points, and the oracle-membership route (v) recovers most of that gap. That would show the gain is in what the tier holds, which timing does not predict.
newIdeas.revised_kill_criterion:
Kill in any of these cases:
- With content fixed, every route lands within 3 points of every other at every query delay on LongMemEval-S. Routing would then not matter, and the claim cannot be tested.
- The paired CI half-width stays above 2 points at the 150-to-300-question scale the budget allows.
- A full read of MemTools (2607.21404) or of 2601.01280's organization-stage tables shows a published content-matched comparison of tiers against a temporal rule.

Downgrade to a note inside #5 if the only non-trivial system, T-B, turns out to be the dropped 'pinned core memory' question with no timing story. That happens if the timing AUC is below 0.6 and the tier advantage is under 2 points.
newIdeas.fold_target: #5 (Update frequency is not retention). This is the external-store arm of the same claim that a tier is only a timescale, and the recency quota plays the role of #5's fast-level decay. If the pilot shows no sensitivity to routing, fold the CPU-only membership test (the AUC of timing features for core-block membership) into #5 as a side result and drop the rest. In Arc 3 it sits beside #10. It differs from #6, which reserves a quota per collision group rather than by time.

original.title: Tiers or timing? A content-matched test of whether short- and long-term agent memory reduce to formation, evolution and retrieval (F/E/R) schedules
original.one_liner: Cache every formation and consolidation call of tiered memories (a FIFO working buffer plus a consolidating store, a MemGPT-style core block plus an archive, and LightMem), so the stored content is identical across variants. Then replace the tier boundary with single-store rules based only on time (a recency quota, ACT-R-style activation) and test whether timing alone reproduces what the tiers do.
original.survey_cell: Working x Token-level against Factual/Experiential x Token-level. The survey's figure equates short-term with working memory and long-term with factual plus experiential. Dynamics: when F, E and R are invoked.
original.survey_hook: The survey's position, known only from search snippets and not checked in the PDF: short-term and long-term memory 'emerge from the temporal patterns with which formation, evolution and retrieval are engaged', not from separate modules, and F/E/R 'need not be invoked at every time step'. Yet Section 7.8 observes that current designs mirror the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model. Systems in the survey's list build explicit tiers: MemGPT (2310.08560), LightMem (2510.18866) and Multiple Memory Systems (2508.15294). AgeMem (2601.01885) learns unified long- and short-term management by RL. A Simple Yet Strong Baseline (2511.17208) is the brute-force reference for the complexity-bias critique. Novelty is unverified: the three-search budget went to ideas 1-2, so search for a content-matched ablation of tiers against a single store before committing.
original.big_picture_hook: The doc's main bet is memory that works on several timescales, built inside the model (Nested Learning/HOPE, whose levels differ only in update frequency) or outside it (Memini's fast and slow edge variables). The survey's position is the strong form of that bet: a tier is nothing but a timescale. Card #5 tests this inside the model and finds that update frequency alone yields lagged copies unless the fast level decays. This card tests the same claim in the external store, where the analogue of decay is a recency quota. The doc's third lesson (old and new experiences compete at retrieval, 2604.27003) predicts that a tier's real job is to reserve context for recent items.
original.task:
Benchmarks:
- LoCoMo: 10 long conversations with their QA set.
- LongMemEval-S: 500 questions, with histories of about 115k tokens.
- A 100-question LongMemEval-M subset (about 500 sessions) as a roughly 10x tempo shift.

Stability is accuracy on questions whose evidence sits in early sessions. Plasticity is accuracy on the knowledge-update and temporal-reasoning categories.

Metrics:
- Official LongMemEval judge accuracy and LoCoMo F1/judge, both at matched context tokens.
- A paired-bootstrap equivalence margin of plus or minus 2 points.
- The share of accuracy variance explained by schedule versus routing (eta squared).
- Each family's stability-plasticity frontier.
original.mechanism:
One shared harness. The formation and consolidation LLM is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on vLLM (or gpt-4o-mini by API), the embedder is bge-small, and the same model reads.

Tiered systems:
- T-A: a FIFO working buffer of K turns always in context, plus a vector store consolidated every tau_E sessions.
- T-B: a MemGPT-style core block of at most B tokens curated by the agent, plus an archival store.
- T-C: LightMem's released code, if it runs on the local backbone.

Step 1: Run each tiered system once per schedule, tau_E in {1, 4, 16 sessions, end-only}. Cache every F and E call and its output.

Step 2: Route the identical cached items four ways, with no new formation calls:
(i) the original tiers;
(ii) a single store with similarity top-k;
(iii) the same plus a quota of the q most recently formed items;
(iv) the same plus ACT-R-style base-level activation: the sum of (t - t_j)^-d over the item's formation and re-access events, where a re-access is a hit in the similarity lookup at write time.
The temporal rules have at most 2 parameters, fit on a dev split. Because the content is byte-identical, any gap is attributable to the tier boundary itself.

Step 3: On LongMemEval-M, compare how well each setting tuned on S transfers: tier capacity K (in tokens) against q and d (expressed per topic segment).
original.hypothesis:
H1, the survey's position: for each tiered system and schedule, the best single-store temporal rule comes within plus or minus 2 points of the tiers on both benchmarks.

H2: The schedule tau_E explains at least twice as much accuracy variance as the routing, and the tiered family's stability-plasticity frontier lies inside the activation family's.

H3: The agent-curated MemGPT core block is the hardest case, because its membership comes from judged importance, not time. If activation still matches it within 2 points, importance can be recovered from re-access timing.

The refutation is also publishable: a tier beats every temporal rule by at least 4 points, and the gap localizes to items whose importance does not show up in re-access.
original.first_experiment:
About 10 GPU-h plus about $20 of judge API:
- Run T-A and T-B at tau_E in {1, end-only} on LoCoMo and 200 LongMemEval-S questions, caching formation.
- Evaluate routes (i) to (iv).

GO if all three hold:
1. The routes differ by at least 3 points somewhere, so the benchmark is sensitive to routing.
2. The paired CI half-width is at most 2 points.
3. The temporal rules either come within 2 points of the tiers (support) or trail by at least 4 points (refutation).

On GO, run the schedule sweep and the shift to the M subset.
original.kill_criterion:
Kill if, with content fixed, every route (plain similarity top-k included) lands within 3 points of every other on both benchmarks. Routing would then not matter there, and the claim cannot be tested on them.

Also kill if two seeds give CI half-widths above 2 points at the affordable sample size, or if a search before committing finds a published content-matched ablation of tiers against a single store.

headline_changes: The survey supplies framing, not novelty. Its paper list stops around January 2026 and contains no streaming-3D work. It also leaves out every 2025-26 direct competitor (BetaEdit/OrthoEdit/EvoEdit, Dual-Layer, EVAF, Scal3R, Free Geometry), so a sparse cell reflects the survey's scope, not open ground. Every novelty verdict still rests on the earlier targeted searches, and the open must-reads still gate their cards: BetaEdit's analysis section and 2606.26783 for #1, ALLOT for #9, and the RGMem code for #10.

The portfolio shrinks from 17 cards to 13 standing projects. #7 and #13 merge into #2: #13's probes become #2's measurement and verification layer, and #7 becomes #2's phase-2 'which form should a kept scene take' paper. The new generate/retrieve router also goes into #2's measurement layer. #14 and the new 'consolidation debt' measurement both fold into #9, as its noise/corroboration arm and its measured expiry cost. #16 is dropped because the survey gives it no leverage and it is the card furthest from the thesis.

Tier moves. #3 drops from A to B: survey-listed rivals (SELF-PARAM writes, address-selected parameter blocks from 'Pretraining with hierarchical memories') threaten it, and reading it against the survey exposed three design flaws (atomic facts save at most about 3x in tokens, the NL stub duplicates the question, and 'passes with full text' is not 'hidden in the weights'). #6, #9 and #11 drop from B to C. #8 rises to the top of Tier B once rescoped to a black-box read-side guarantee at 25-40 GPU-h: none of the 46 experiential-token works certifies non-regression against no-memory, so this is the cleanest gap the survey reveals.

Several headlines are rewritten as falsifiable tests of named survey positions, replacing method claims. #1: protected-set editors implement Formation, not Updating, shown as a 2x2 against the survey-listed PEAK append case. #5: forgetting, not update frequency, creates a long-term store. The old 'HOPE is degenerate' headline is probably wrong, because HOPE's Titans fast level already has a decay gate and momentum. #10 becomes theory-first: k*(h,eps) predicts that RGMem's 'invariant' theta=3 moves. #12 tests Scissorhands' persistence-of-importance hypothesis. #4's main result becomes the memory horizon as a function of replay fraction.

Strong baselines from the survey list are now mandatory, and each could kill a card. MemRL utility re-ranking for #6 and #8. SELF-PARAM KL context integration for #3, #7 and #11. The Memory^3 frequency hierarchy for #9, which turns out to be the uncited static case of rent-or-buy. RGMem and Memory-R1 for #10. Context-as-Memory FOV-selected frames at matched bytes for #2 and #4, plus reset-and-rebuild (IterResearch) for #4. ACE delta updates for #8 and #15. Embodied VideoAgent for #17. Zep-style invalidation for #1 and #9.

Mapping the cards exposed internal errors, now fixed. In #2 the eviction-budget sweep is unmotivated, since a snapshot is about 1 MB and storage was never the constraint. #11's storage advantage is false at N<=100, and its bottom-up refit contradicts 'no text kept'. On homogeneous streams #10's Bayes gate is just a tuned count threshold, so its old kill test would fail by construction. #1's plan misdescribes WISE. In #7, per-scene adapters are not consolidation, because they cannot interfere with each other.

Compute now respects the <=1.5B / ~200 GPU-h-per-paper constraint everywhere: Llama3-8B is dropped from #1 and Qwen3-8B from #8 and #15. Estimates: #2 about 100, #5 40-60, #8 25-40, #10 30-40, #9 about 75, #11 75-90 and #4 about 100 GPU-h. The A+B pilots together cost under about 60 GPU-h.

Four new survey-driven ideas survive adversarial checks, none above Tier B. 'Ghosts in the pointer memory' enters B: stale entries in explicit learned 3D memory after the world changes, gated by a 6 GPU-h oracle-deletion test. The start-state pool, the RL-manager swap audit and 'tiers or timing' enter Tier C. The prequential generate/retrieve router and consolidation debt are folded into #2 and #9, because their headline claims are partly scooped (2608.29705 calibration audit, ClashEval).

Decision at week 3:
- #1 GO: it becomes paper 1.
- #2 GO: Arc 1 becomes the main line. Run the Ghosts H1 oracle gate (6 GPU-h) on #2's 3RScan pipeline, and #7 follows as phase 2.
- #2 killed (byte-matched frames come within 2 points): run Ghosts H1 anyway, and weigh Arc 2 via #3's 0.6B pilot, but only after SELF-PARAM and the LoRA-bank check.

arcs: Arc 1, streaming 3D as a memory system (main line if #2 passes). #2 (with #13's probes and the G/R router) asks whether the state is memory or a cache, and what happens when the world changes. #7, as #2's phase 2, asks which form a kept scene should take. #4 asks whether rehearsal extends the state's horizon at equal passes. Ghosts covers stale explicit 3D memory under world change. #12 is the KV diagnostic. The start-state pool (C) is cross-scene experience. Unifying survey test: whether short- and long-term memory in a frozen recurrent 3D model emerge from F/E/R timing (persist, rehearse, restore, evict) or need a change of form or store. Shared infrastructure: one TTT3R fork with state-dump, read-only raymap and injection hooks; 7-Scenes/12-Scenes/TUM revisit pairs; a 3RScan change pipeline.

Arc 2, the life cycle of a fact across store and weights. #1 (lead): the weights have no DELETE, and a ledger supplies it. #3: when can the store copy be demoted to an index. #9 (with #14 and consolidation debt): when to move a changing fact into the weights, and what expiry costs. Unifying survey hook: the token-parametric synchronization gap the survey glosses over. Token-level stores have CRUD and Zep-style invalidation; parametric memory has only ADD. Shared: GPT2-XL/phi-1.5/Qwen2.5-0.5-1.5B, EasyEdit/AlphaEdit/BetaEdit, CounterFact/AToKe/PEAK/TOFU/WikiBigEdit, and Zep-style validity records. #1's salvage cost feeds #9, and #3's per-fact reachability logs feed #9's simulator.

Arc 3, timescale theory (cheapest; tests the survey's central STM/LTM claim most directly). #5: inside the model, forgetting rather than update frequency makes a long-term level. #11: same-module vs separate store for folded session states, mapped against per-head decay. #10: the overwrite threshold k*(h,eps) and the entrenchment law in external stores. Tiers-or-timing (C): whether an external memory tier is just a recency prior. Shared: flash-linear-attention, delta-rule algebra, a session-reset MQAR harness and CPU simulations. #10's hazard estimator is shared with #9.

Arc 4, trustworthy experiential and agent memory (secondary, API-heavy, GPU-light). #8 (lead): certified retrieval timing, i.e. a do-no-harm guarantee against no-memory. #15: lineage depth explains context collapse. #6: attributing BWT loss to F, E and R. The RL manager audit (as #10's baselines, or standalone). #17 stands alone in Arc 4's spirit, as a complexity-bias test on 3D episodic memory. Shared: Dynamic Cheatsheet/ACE/ExpeL/MemRL builders, cached no-memory arms, ALFWorld and Hidden-Rule World.
survey_positions_we_test: 'Short- vs long-term memory emerge from the temporal patterns of formation, evolution and retrieval, not from separate modules' [SNIP]. Primary tests: #5 (forgetting vs frequency factorial), #4 (memory horizon vs replay fraction) and #11 (same-module vs separate-store fold mapped against decay). Secondary tests: #2/#7 (persist the state vs change its form), #12 (revisit-gap strata) and tiers-or-timing. Verify the wording in the PDF before any card makes it a headline. Do not let all of these cards claim to test it.
Model editing is the Updating operator for parametric memory [SNIP]. #1 predicts that history-aware protected-set editors are append-only Formation and need an explicit forgetting step (PEAK 2x2).

Parametric memory is efficient but suffers catastrophic forgetting [SEC]. #1 predicts the opposite failure for revised facts (over-retention). #3 separates storage loss from access loss. #7 phase 2's shared-adapter arm is the only place real interference can appear.
Token-level (non-parametric) memory sidesteps forgetting (survey-listed HippoRAG 2 framing). #6 tests whether forgetting moves into retrieval displacement.

7.2/7.3: memory management should move from heuristics to learned, RL-trained policies. #8: do learned utilities hold a harm budget without calibration? #10: does a derived gate match a learned UPDATE/NOOP gate on small calibration data? RL audit: is the RL gain learned writing or learned deciding? #9: analytic index vs bandit.
7.1: from memory retrieval to memory generation. #3: an address cues regeneration from the weights. #2's router asks when a generated raymap view should be trusted over retrieved keyframes.
Latent memory is efficient but opaque, possibly 'just caching' [SEC]. #2's byte- and pass-matched state vs re-fed frames frontier; #13's read-only probes with prior control.

The emphasis on strategy-based (distilled) experiential memory. #8 measures harm by abstraction level, #15 predicts an interior optimal distillation depth, and #6 tests whether abstraction raises collision density.
Survey-listed Memory^3's frequency-based memory hierarchy. #9 predicts that frequency-only placement fails for volatile, frequently queried facts.
Survey-listed Scissorhands' persistence-of-importance hypothesis. #12 tests it on long-gap 3D revisits; Ghosts tests it under world change.
Survey-listed RGMem's dataset-invariant critical threshold theta=3. #10 predicts it moves with hazard and noise.

Token-level topology grading (flat/planar/hierarchical) and the complexity-bias critique [SEC]. #17 runs a topology x operator test against uniform subsampling. Brute-force rows: #1 compaction, #8 compute-matched sc@k, #11 bank+route, #2 re-fed frames.
caveats: The survey itself was never read. The PDF and arXiv are blocked here. Everything comes from the companion repo's two figures and its README paper list (commit 4b45128, Mar 2026), the abstract, TOC fragments, search snippets, and third-party summaries. Positions marked [SEC], such as the forgetting trade-off and the complexity-bias and sync-gap critiques, may not be the survey's own claims. Quotes marked [SNIP], including the 'temporal patterns' claim many cards build on, must be checked in the PDF before they are quoted in any paper.

Cell counts were tallied from the README by Function x Form and are approximate; a paper can appear in several cells. A sparse cell means the survey did not cover it, not that the area is novel. The list stops around January 2026, omits all streaming-3D work, and misses the 2025-26 direct competitors (BetaEdit/OrthoEdit/EvoEdit, Dual-Layer, EVAF, Scal3R, Free Geometry, ProtoDepth).

Many overlap descriptions rest only on search snippets: MemRL, ReMe, RGMem's theta, Hindsight, M+, Memory^3, ACE's collapse numbers, PEAK, WISE and ELDER internals. Argos-SLAM (2610.10181) was seen in one snippet and not re-found. 2609.24238 could not be verified at all and must not be cited. R3Mem, LightMem and Timeline-memory details are recalled, not checked.

Survey vocabulary (F/E/R, cells, frontiers) helps position work for agent-memory venues, but it adds no novelty. 3D venues (#2, #4, #12, Ghosts) will judge on 3D baselines, not on taxonomy. Several cards also now 'test' the same STM/LTM sentence, which reviewers will see as framing inflation if overused.

The survey framing makes 'why not just keep it in a token-level store?' the obvious reviewer question for every parametric card (#1, #3, #9). Each needs an in-context or time-aware RAG reference row and a stated reason that parametric storage matters (closed-book, on-device, or consolidation).

GPU estimates are planning numbers that assume hooks work on the first attempt. Before any pilot, confirm the CUT3R raymap update=False path and the 768x768 state size, BetaEdit code support for GPT2-XL, and the Memalpha-4B checkpoint's provenance. API model names and costs for #8, #10 and the audit need re-checking at run time.
Merging #7 and #13 into #2 risks scope creep. Keep #2's paper to the cross-session cache test plus the updating section, at about 100 GPU-h, and hold #7's form comparison for a second paper.

Tiers reflect novelty plus feasibility under the stated constraints, not certainty. Every A/B card still has an explicit early kill clause, and two of them (#1's z-margin absorption, #2's byte-matched frames coming within 2 points) could fail in the first pilot.
